name: Interview behavioural questions, set 5
description: Spoken behavioural questions with model answers and rubrics: a failed risk, an unpopular call, an unasked problem, a first-year's day, a bet with unknown odds, a project redo, a new direction and a short lesson. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: the risk that failed.

widget.prompt: Tell me about a risk you took that did not pay off.
widget.model: In my second year I was treasurer of the university hockey club, and I booked a hall for 150 people for our end-of-season dinner. We usually booked for 90. Ticket sales had grown about 30% a year, and I judged we had roughly a 60% chance of filling it. If we did, the club would clear £900 towards new kit. If we did not, the deposit and fixed costs meant a loss of up to £400. I put those numbers to the committee and they agreed. Then exam dates moved, many second-team players went home early, and we sold 104 tickets. The club lost £310 on the night. I would take the same bet again, because the odds and the sizes were sound when I took it. What I changed was the structure. I now pay a smaller refundable deposit and set a date by which we can scale down, so a miss costs far less.

rubric.text: Answers in the first sentence or two: the risk you took and the setting
The odds as you saw them at the time, given as a chance or a comparison
The loss or shortfall stated as a number
Separates the decision from the outcome: what you would repeat and why
One concrete change you made afterwards
Under 300 words, told in the order it happened

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: The interviewer is testing whether you judge a decision by its odds rather than its result. State the chance and the stakes as you saw them before the outcome. Then say what you would keep and what you changed.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: the unpopular decision.

widget.prompt: Describe a decision of yours that was unpopular with the group.
widget.model: In my third year I led a five-person coursework group with two weeks to model local house prices. The other four wanted a neural network, because it looked impressive. I decided against it. We had 2,000 sales, and a quick test I ran showed the network beat a plain regression by under 1% while taking about three days to tune. I said so at our Monday meeting, with the two error figures on one slide, and offered to write up the comparison myself. Two people were annoyed, and one said I was playing it safe, so I asked her to rerun my comparison herself. We kept the regression and spent those three days checking the data. We found 140 duplicated sales, which had moved our main coefficient by 12%. The marker singled out that check, and we got 74%. Later a teammate pointed out that the duplicates would have misled the network too. I learned to bring a number to a disagreement, not just a view.

rubric.text: Answers early: the decision, and who was against it
Your reason at the time, backed by a fact or a number
How and when you told the group, in the first person
The result, set against the option the group wanted
Admits the cost: who was unhappy and how you handled it
Under 300 words, told in the order it happened

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A strong answer shows a decision made on evidence and explained openly, not one forced through. Name the cost to the group honestly. Then compare the result with what the other option would have given.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: the problem nobody asked about.

widget.prompt: Tell me about a problem you spotted that nobody had asked you to look for.
widget.model: Last summer I had a part-time job in a bike shop's back office, entering repair jobs. Nobody had asked me to look at stock. I noticed that we kept telling customers our most common inner tube was out, about one week in four. One lunchtime I put three months of sales and delivery dates into a spreadsheet. The reorder point had been set on the previous year's sales, which had since risen by about 40%. That Friday, before the next order went in, I gave the manager a one-page summary. I suggested raising the reorder point from 20 tubes to 30 and checking it every quarter. She agreed to try it for a month. That month we had no stock-outs, and tube sales were about £300 higher than in the same month a year before. She then asked me to run the same check on brake pads. I now look at the records behind any task I am given.

rubric.text: Answers early: the problem you found, and that no one had asked
How you noticed it and how you checked that it was real
Whom you told and when, and what you proposed
What changed afterwards, with a number
Raised it with the person responsible rather than acting alone
Under 300 words, told in the order it happened

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: The interviewer wants initiative with judgement: you checked before you spoke, then took it to the right person. Give the evidence in a sentence or two. End on what changed, with a number.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: a first-year's working day.

widget.prompt: What do you think a first-year in this role does all day, and which part would you find hardest?
widget.model: From two traders I met at a careers evening and from the firm's own talks, I picture the day in three parts. Before the open, a first-year checks overnight moves, the desk's positions and the events due that day. During the session they watch risk on a few products, adjust quotes within limits a senior trader sets, and answer the desk's questions quickly. After the close they check the day's trades and profit, and write a short note on what moved and why. Around that there is project work, such as a small tool or a study of fills that lost money. The part I expect to find hardest is speed when the information is noisy. I can be slow when I want to be certain. I now play one timed estimation round a day and log it, and my share answered inside the limit has risen from half to four in five. In the first month I would also ask for direct feedback on where I hesitate.

rubric.text: Answers the question asked: what the day holds, not why the firm is good
Three or more concrete tasks spread across the day
Says where the picture comes from: people met, talks or reading
One honest weakness that matters in this role
A specific step already taken against that weakness
Under 300 words

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: This question tests whether your interest rests on facts about the job. Name tasks, not values, and say where you learned them. Pick a weakness that is real for the role and show what you already do about it.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: a bet with unknown odds.

widget.prompt: I offer you a bet and I will not tell you the odds. What do you ask me before you decide? You have two minutes.
widget.model: I would ask four things, in order of how much they change my decision. First, what exactly do I win and what do I lose? Without both amounts I cannot price the bet at all. Second, who set the terms, and do you know more than I do? You chose to offer it, so I assume you have an edge, and I need a margin to cover that. Third, can I play more than once? If the bet repeats, early results tell me about the odds, so a small first stake buys information. Fourth, what is the most I can lose in total? That caps my stake whatever the odds turn out to be. My rule would be this. If the win is at least three times the stake, my loss is capped and I can repeat, I take a small stake and update as I go. If you set the terms and I get one play only, I decline unless the payout is far above anything a fair bet would give.

rubric.text: Asks first about the amounts won and lost
Asks who set the terms and allows for that side's edge
Asks whether the bet repeats and what one play would teach
Asks for a cap on the total loss before deciding
Ends with a decision rule that says when you would bet
Questions in a stated order, short enough for two minutes

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: There is no single right list; the test is the order of your questions. The payout and the other side's knowledge matter most, then repetition and a cap on loss. End with a rule, so the interviewer hears a decision.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: the project decision to redo.

widget.prompt: Which decision in your project would you make differently now, and what would it change?
widget.model: My final-year project forecast next-day footfall at one railway station from weather and calendar data. The decision I would change is how I split the data. I shuffled the days at random into training and test sets. That let the model learn from the days either side of each test day, which share their weather. My test error was 2.8%, which looked excellent. In my last month I retrained on the earlier years only and tested on the final year. The error rose to 4.9%, barely better than copying the same weekday a week earlier. That gap was the evidence that my split had leaked information. If I did it again, I would split by time from the start and test on a rolling window. I would then have spent the time on features that help, such as holiday effects, instead of tuning a model whose score was inflated. I reported the honest figure of 4.9% in my write-up, with the leak explained.

rubric.text: Names one decision of your own, early and plainly
The evidence that it was wrong, with a number
What you would do instead, specifically
The size of the effect, before and after
What the redo would have freed time or effort for
Owns the decision without blaming tools, data or a supervisor

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: Interviewers ask this to see whether you can audit your own work. Pick a real decision, show the evidence against it and put a size on the effect. Saying what you reported afterwards shows you can be trusted with results.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: your change of direction.

widget.prompt: Take me through the change of direction on your CV.
widget.model: I started a degree in chemistry and moved to mathematics and statistics after my first year. The reason at the time was simple. The part of chemistry I enjoyed most was the data analysis in lab reports, not the lab work itself. I scored 82% in the first-year statistics module and 61% in practical chemistry, and I took that seriously. The switch cost me a year, because I had to repeat two first-year maths modules. A lot carried over. Lab work taught me to keep careful records and to distrust a result I could not repeat. I use that when I test code: I write down what I expect before I run it. Chemistry also gave me a feel for rates and equilibria, which helped in differential equations. The move was a decision on evidence about where I was strongest, and I would make it again.

rubric.text: States the change and when it happened, in the first sentence or two
The reason you had at the time, backed by a fact
At least two things that carried over, with an example of one
Names the cost of the change plainly
No apology for the change
Under 300 words, told in the order it happened

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: An interviewer asks this to see whether you can explain a choice without defending it. Give the reason you had then, name the cost and show what carried over. Ending on the decision, not an apology, reads as judgement.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: teach me something you know.

widget.prompt: You have thirty seconds to prepare and ninety seconds to answer. Teach me something you know well that I probably do not.
widget.model: I will teach you to read the wind from a weather map. The curved lines on the map are isobars, which join places with the same air pressure. Wind blows roughly along those lines, not straight across them. In the northern hemisphere it circles anticlockwise round an area of low pressure. The closer the lines, the stronger the wind. Here is an example. Picture a low over Scotland with lines packed tightly to its south. The flow on that southern side runs from west to east, so England gets strong westerly winds. If you cycled from Bristol to London that day, you would have the wind behind you. Now a check that you followed. If the low sat over France instead, which way would the wind blow over London? It would come from the east, because London is on the northern side of an anticlockwise flow. That is the whole idea.

rubric.text: One idea, named in the first sentence
One worked example that applies the idea
A question that checks the listener followed, with its answer
Plain words, with each term explained when it first appears
Ends within two sentences of the check
Under 250 words, which fits ninety seconds spoken

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A recorded answer has no one to ask you questions, so build the check into it. Choose one idea small enough for ninety seconds, give one example, then test the listener. Plain words matter more than a clever topic.
